To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

JOLs are insensitive to the anticipated forgetting interval unless participants are asked to estimate recall probabilities for different retention intervals, and that when they are asked to do this, JOLs mimic actual recall probabilities.

JOLs do not reflect the amount of forgetting expected to occur between encoding and test, unless people are explicitly asked to predict forgetting, and that people's estimates of forgetting do not reflect the actual forgetting that occurs unless people are explicitly instructed to think about forgetting.
JOLs are insensitive to retention interval unless participants are prompted to make a theory-based prediction of their recall rate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether people can make accurate predictions of their own forgetting.
the role of experience in the formation and use of subjective probability judgments.
the role of experience in the development of intuitive theory, and with the role of theory in intuitive judgment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the role of experience-based processes in JOLs is to predict recall, whereas the role of theory-based processes is to predict retention.
JOLs reflect the operation of both theory- and experience-based processes, and the balance between these two processes can be influenced by the task and the instructions provided to participants.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

JOLs are sensitive to a number of variables that affect learning, including the type of task, the nature of the material, the amount of study, and the amount of prior knowledge, but they are not sensitive to the retention interval unless participants are asked to predict recall rates across a number of retention intervals.
the JOLs are not based on memory, but are based on the experience of the learner.
people can make accurate judgments of learning if they are able to access their knowledge about the factors that influence forgetting, but only if the notion of forgetting itself is made salient.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the distinction between experience- and theory-based processes can be used to understand the nature of JOLs.
JOLs are sensitive to the retention interval, but only when people have the opportunity to make theory-based predictions of their future performance.
people are able to make predictions that are based on their knowledge of how well they will remember things, but that they are only able to do so when that knowledge is made salient to them.
